listening.passage: Receptionist: Good morning, City College language centre, booking office. How can I help you?  Student: Oh hello. My name is Jenny Chen, I would like to ask about the short course in Marketing Communication that you run every term. Receptionist: Of course. Which intake were you interested in? It starts on the 8th of December and finishes on the 26th. Student: That sounds good. How many weeks is it, and what days? Receptionist: It runs for three weeks, every Tuesday and Thursday evening, from 6:30 to 8:30. The maximum group size is twelve students, and we keep it small so everyone gets feedback. Student: Great. And where exactly is the class held? Receptionist: In the North Building, room 204, just opposite the main library. Student: I see. How much is the fee? Receptionist: The full fee is 380 dollars, but if you book before the end of this month you get a 10 percent early-bird discount, so you would pay 342. Student: I would like to take the early-bird offer. What does the course include? Receptionist: Everything is included: ten hours of tuition, the textbook Marketing Essentials, weekly practice tests and one individual tutorial with the tutor. Student: What about books to buy myself? Receptionist: Nothing else is needed. However, if you want to keep Marketing Essentials, you can buy it after the course at half price from the college bookshop. Student: Lovely. Now, what if I finish work late and cannot attend one session? Receptionist: Each student can miss up to two sessions and we make them up the following week during the lunch break. Student: That is very flexible. How do I pay, and how do I confirm? Receptionist: You pay when you arrive, in cash or by card, but we need your confirmation by Friday. You can confirm online through the enrolment form on our website, or you can email me directly. Student: I will confirm online this evening. Can you tell me the tutor's name and background? Receptionist: The tutor is Dr Marcus Whitfield. He worked as a brand manager for a global cosmetics company before he started teaching here four years ago. He is known for practical cases and lots of role-plays. Student: Sounds perfect. One last question: is there a certificate at the end? Receptionist: Yes, all students who attend at least 80 percent of the sessions receive a certificate of completion. Student: Excellent. I will book now. My email is jenny.chen2026 at mail dot com. Receptionist: Let me note that down: jenny dot chen 2026 at mail dot com. Is that correct? Student: Yes, exactly. Thank you very much. Receptionist: You are welcome, and good luck with the course.

listening.passage: Today's lecture continues our series on study skills. I want to share five evidence-based strategies that consistently improve results: retrieval practice, spaced repetition, interleaving, elaboration and focused attention. Let us take them one by one. First, retrieval practice. Actively trying to recall information from memory is far more powerful than re-reading your notes. You can close the book and write everything you remember about a topic, or use self-testing with flashcards. Re-reading creates a false sense of fluency, whereas testing exposes the gaps in your memory and forces the brain to reconstruct knowledge. Research shows students who use retrieval practice remember about 50 percent more after one week than those who only re-read. Second, spaced repetition means spacing your practice sessions out over time instead of cramming the night before. A review that took place one day, three days and one week after first learning is far more effective. Your brain consolidates memories during sleep, so all-night revision is actively counterproductive. Third, interleaving means mixing different topics or problem types within one study session, rather than studying Topic A for two hours and then Topic B for two hours. Interleaving feels harder in the moment, but it dramatically improves your ability to distinguish between problem types in the exam. Fourth, elaboration means explaining the material in your own words, connecting new concepts to what you already know, or even teaching it to someone else. Feynman's rule: if you cannot explain it in plain English, you do not understand it yet. Drawing mind-maps and asking 'why' repeatedly also help build deeper understanding. Fifth, focused attention. Divided attention is the enemy of deep learning. Switching between textbook and phone can cut your learning efficiency by up to 60 percent. Use timed sessions of 25 minutes, called the Pomodoro technique, take five-minute breaks for movement and water, and keep your phone in another room. To summarise, the ingredients of effective study are: recall from memory, spaced review, mixed practice, explaining in your own words, and full attention for short sprints. Replace one re-reading habit with one of these this week, and measure the difference yourself. Any questions before the next class?

part1.q: Do you work or are you a student? Tell me about it.
part1.ref: I'm currently working as a junior accountant in a logistics company. It's my first full-time job after graduation, and I mainly handle invoices and monthly ledgers, which I find quite satisfying.

part1.q: What do you like most about your job or studies?
part1.ref: What I like most is that every week teaches me something new. Dealing with real clients makes the work meaningful, and I'm improving my communication skills every day.

part1.q: Would you like to change your job or major in the future? Why or why not?
part1.ref: Not at the moment. I still have a lot to learn in this field, and changing too quickly would waste the experience I've already built up.

part1.q: Do you think your subject or job will be useful in the future?
part1.ref: Absolutely. Financial literacy matters in every industry, so even if I switch companies or countries one day, these skills will always travel with me.

part1.q: What do you usually do after work or classes?
part1.ref: Usually I read for half an hour and then go for a walk. It clears my mind completely, and it helps me sleep better at night.

part1.q: Where is your hometown and what is it like?
part1.ref: My hometown is a mid-sized city in the Yangtze River delta. It's known for its canals, relaxed pace of life and the little snacks sold along the riverbank.

part1.q: What do you like most about your hometown?
part1.ref: I like the calm riverside and the neighbourhood markets in the evenings, where everyone knows each other and dinner is always fresh and cheap.

part1.q: Is there anything you dislike about your hometown?
part1.ref: The traffic in summer is terrible, honestly. The roads are narrow and when the rain comes the whole city moves at a walking pace.

part1.q: Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
part1.ref: Hugely. New metro lines and a riverfront park went in last year, so it's now much easier to get around and there are more weekend events.

part1.q: Would you like to live in your hometown in the future?
part1.ref: Maybe for a few years, but I'd rather see more of the world first. My hometown is comfortable, but comfort can also become a very small world.

part1.q: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
part1.ref: I live in a two-bedroom apartment on the eighth floor, with a small balcony overlooking the neighbourhood garden. It's quiet and well connected to the bus line.

part1.q: What is your favourite part of your home?
part1.ref: My desk by the window. The morning light hits it perfectly, and it's where I do all my reading and video calls — it's basically my private base.

part1.q: Would you like to move to a different kind of home? Why?
part1.ref: One day I'd love a small house with a garden. I miss having plants around me, and a garden would also give me a quiet place to run in the mornings.

part1.q: How is your home different from when you were a child?
part1.ref: Back then we shared a tiny three-room flat with my grandparents. Now I have my own space, my own habits and a lot more quiet — and I really value that.

part1.q: Is it better to live alone or with others, in your opinion?
part1.ref: Short-term I prefer living alone — it's peaceful and you learn to be disciplined. But long-term, living with someone you trust teaches you compromise and warmth.

part1.q: What kind of music do you like listening to?
part1.ref: Mostly indie folk and some old Mandarin rock. I like music with honest lyrics — songs that feel like the writer actually lived the story.

part1.q: Do you play any musical instruments?
part1.ref: Only the guitar, badly. I've been practising for two years — I can play maybe five songs slowly. Progress is slow but the habit is joyful.

part1.q: Has your taste in music changed over time?
part1.ref: Definitely. In school I only listened to pop. Now I prefer quieter songs with acoustic instruments, because they let me concentrate while I work.

part1.q: Do you prefer listening to music alone or with others?
part1.ref: Both, honestly. Alone when I'm studying, with friends at live houses or KTV. Music is how we bond after a long week of work and deadlines.

part1.q: How often do you go to concerts or live shows?
part1.ref: Maybe two or three times a year. Tickets and the crowds are expensive in terms of energy, but a great live show can recharge me for weeks.

part1.q: Do you like reading? What do you read?
part1.ref: Yes, every single night before bed — usually essays or non-fiction on psychology and business. Fiction feels like dessert, non-fiction like a conversation with the author.

part1.q: Do you prefer paper books or e-books?
part1.ref: Paper for long reading sessions, e-ink reader for commuting. Paper has that lovely weight and smell; e-books win on convenience and built-in dictionary.

part1.q: How many books did you read last year?
part1.ref: About a dozen — mostly under 300 pages. I keep a reading log, and the streak matters to me more than the count itself.

part1.q: What do you usually do with a book after you finish it?
part1.ref: I lend it to a friend with a sticky note inside — the best recommendation I ever received was via a borrowed book with handwriting in the margin.

part1.q: Where do you usually read?
part1.ref: In a café with low music and unlimited coffee, or on the window seat on the metro. Somehow the gentle background noise makes pages turn faster.

part1.q: How often do you go shopping?
part1.ref: Once or twice a month in person, but I browse online almost daily — mostly for skincare and books. Buying is rare; researching is a daily habit.

part1.q: Do you prefer shopping alone or with friends?
part1.ref: With friends for clothes — they know my colours and stop me from impulse-buying. Alone for essentials, because friends make grocery trips three times longer.

part1.q: Have you ever bought something you later regretted?
part1.ref: A white linen shirt, impulsively, at midnight. It was expensive and it looked tired after one wash — a classic lazy-buy lesson I repeat every season.

part1.q: What kind of shops are popular in your hometown?
part1.ref: Wet markets and snack streets rule. People queue at 5 pm for the red-bean buns and the dumpling shop that opens only three hours a day.

part1.q: Do you think online shopping will replace physical stores?
part1.ref: For staples, yes — everything arrives in hours. But stores offering experience, like bookshop cafés or demo kitchens, will survive because we shop there for feeling too.

part1.q: What do you usually do in your free time?
part1.ref: I take photos of old streets around Shanghai. It costs nothing and it's become my way of seeing the city slowly, frame by frame.

part1.q: Do you think people nowadays have enough free time?
part1.ref: Not really. Evenings blur into message notifications and weekend plans fill before Friday ends. Real idleness — doing nothing on purpose — is almost a luxury.

part1.q: Would you like to have a hobby that needs more skill?
part1.ref: Yes — pottery. It involves patience, physical feel and forgiving mistakes with your hands. Every bowl teaches you to accept imperfection beautifully.

part1.q: How has your free time changed compared to five years ago?
part1.ref: I used to chase ten hobbies; now I protect two — cooking and running — and I do them deeply. Focus beats variety once you accept you have limited evenings.

part1.q: How do you make plans for your free time?
part1.ref: Loosely. I keep a running list of things that sound delicious — restaurants, exhibitions, long walks — and let friends invite me to the ones we can share.

part1.q: What is the weather usually like in your hometown?
part1.ref: Humid summers with plum rains, cold damp winters, and two magical weeks in October and April. Basically a climate that keeps you guessing your wardrobe daily.

part1.q: Does the weather affect your mood or plans?
part1.ref: Enormously. Grey rainy days make me want films and soup; clear autumn skies make me walk fifteen extra minutes just to stay outside a little longer.

part1.q: What kind of weather do you prefer?
part1.ref: Crisp sunny mornings around 20 degrees — the kind that makes you open windows before you even check your phone. Mild weather is a quiet medicine.

part1.q: Has the weather in your city changed over the years?
part1.ref: Yes — summers are hotter now and sudden downpours are more common. When I was small, the plum rains lasted longer, but now the rain arrives in heavier bursts with thunderstorms.

part1.q: Does rainy weather stop people from going out where you live?
part1.ref: Not anymore. Everyone carries clear umbrellas and shops stay open; only the riverfront saxophonist disappears when the rain starts.

points: And explain why it was memorable
part2.ref: Last October I took an overnight train from Shanghai to Kunming with a friend from work — nineteen hours watching the landscape shift from river delta to misty mountains. We had no Wi-Fi, so we actually talked: about his doctorate, my job fears, the book in his bag. At dawn the train reached the high plateau and the light went golden over the farmland — completely unused to seeing. A journey this long forces you to slow down, share food, and surprisingly, see your companion as a real person for the first time.

part2.card: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
points: Why you want to learn it
And explain what difference it would make
part2.ref: I want to learn to cook Sichuanese dishes properly. Growing up we ordered takeaways; my mother cooked simple Cantonese food at best, so every time I eat out in Chengdu I feel culture envy. I'd start with a weekend class — twice weekly for two months — then practise on colleagues who volunteer as judges. Imagine hosting a dinner where the fish-fragrant aubergine actually tastes like the restaurant. Beyond taste, cooking teaches patience and heat control — two skills that transfer directly into my job, where details decide everything before clients ever see the result.

part2.card: Describe an exciting book you have enjoyed reading.
points: When and where you read it
And explain what you learned from it
part2.ref: The book is 'Folding Beijing'. I read it on the metro during the February travel rush, finishing it in three compartments. It imagines a futuristic city where different social classes share the same space in repeating 24-hour shifts — the rich wake at dawn, the middle class at noon, and labourers at night. What thrilled me was the structure of the story and the politics hiding beneath it. It reframed how I see my own city's inequalities. Since reading it, I notice invisible layers everywhere — in who gets the earliest table, the better seat, the quieter carriage.

part2.card: Describe a piece of technology you use every day.
points: How often and for what you use it
Why it is important to you
And explain what you would do without it
part2.ref: My phone is my entire life — navigation, WeChat groups, payment, camera, dictionary. I use it from waking to sleep, maybe six or seven hours honestly. But the feature I depend on most is the map app in real time: it rescued me in rainstorms in Chongqing, rerouted me around jams, and found me the only open noodle shop at midnight. Without it, I'd miss the bus three times a week and order food badly. Still, I set an app limit: no phone in bed after 12:30, or I lie awake doom-scrolling like everyone else.

part3.q: Do you think exams are the fairest way to measure students' abilities?
part3.ref: Exams measure how you perform under pressure on one particular day, not who you really are. They reward memorisation over real understanding. That said, written exams are cheap to run at scale and hard to fake, so some standard measurement is useful. The fairer model is a blend: a few high-stakes exams plus coursework, presentations and practical projects that sample your abilities across the term. Pure exam pressure tells you little about a student's creativity, teamwork or practical judgement.

part3.q: Should schools pay more attention to practical skills than to academic knowledge?
part3.ref: Both matter, but the balance is off. Schools produce exam-fit students who freeze on a form, a contract or a team conflict. Adding mandatory practical courses — financial literacy, conflict resolution, basic cooking or first aid — would change young people's lives far more than one more formula to memorise. Academic knowledge is the map; practical skill is the driving test. A map without driving practice is nearly useless in an emergency.

part3.q: Do you think online education will replace traditional classrooms?
part3.ref: For motivated adult learners, absolutely — platforms now deliver world-class lectures to a bedroom in a county town. But for most teenagers, school is also social training: discipline, friendship, teamwork and handling boredom. Online can supplement, but replacing the social layer would produce a generation of brilliant solo learners who cannot survive a meeting. Hybrid will win, not pure online.

part3.q: What makes a good teacher, in your view?
part3.ref: A good teacher changes how you think, not just what you know. They notice when you're lost before you do, ask you the question you're avoiding, and treat mistakes as information instead of shame. My best teachers shared three habits: they explained patiently, they told stories from real life, and they made you feel the answer belonged to you. Caring plus craft beats qualifications alone.

part3.q: Should university education be free for everyone?
part3.ref: Free tuition would widen access for students from poorer families, and society recovers the investment through taxation later. But zero cost usually means rationing by exam score, which hurts creative or vocational students. A smarter model is full scholarships for the bottom third of income plus generous income-contingent loans like Australia. Education should be affordable and ambitious, not merely free and crowded.

part3.q: How important is lifelong learning in today's economy?
part3.ref: In a world where software rewrites jobs every five years, one degree is a snapshot, not a career plan. Lifelong learning is now the baseline licence to stay relevant — it protects older workers whose expertise expires and helps young workers avoid obsolete specialisms. The future belongs to people who stay curious in public, learning in communities, not just alone at a screen.

part3.q: Do you think technology has made people more alone or more connected?
part3.ref: Both directions at once. Video calls stitch distant families together nightly — my grandmother and I watch opera together across 1,000 kilometres. But feed culture replaces depth with scrolling, and many 'connected' people eat alone headphones-in. The tool doesn't decide; how you use it does. Presence in your own home matters more than presence in the cloud.

part3.q: Will artificial intelligence make many jobs disappear?
part3.ref: AI will absorb routine work fastest — data entry, basic drafting, simple translation. But jobs built on trust, taste and physical presence — carers, negotiators, great teachers — will persist. The real divide is not jobs but tasks. The people who redefine their work around judgement and care will thrive; those who only memorise will be automated out by breakfast.

part3.q: Do you think people spend too much time on social media?
part3.ref: Yes — average daily use keeps climbing past three hours, and nobody feels better after. Social media is engineered like a casino: variable rewards, infinite scroll. Used for news, network and work it's powerful; used as default anaesthetic for every boredom pang, it erodes attention span and sleep. The fix is friction — timers, grey scale, one-screen rooms — not total abstinence, which never lasts.

part3.q: Should there be more regulation of technology companies?
part3.ref: Yes, but smart regulation beats blunt bans. Require transparency for recommendation algorithms, data portability across platforms, age-appropriate design for under-16, and independent audits. Europe is experimenting with the AI Act; China requires algorithm registration. The industry's self-regulation failed publicly for fifteen years. Regulation done well raises trust; done badly, it freezes innovation — neither extreme is acceptable.

part3.q: How has technology changed the way people shop?
part3.ref: Shopping went from a Saturday errand to a background process. Now price comparison happens in seconds, authentic reviews steer choices, and delivery fits in an hour in big cities. Physical stores survive as experience centres — try, entertain, then order online. The skill shift is real: modern shoppers need scepticism for fake reviews and discipline for one-click impulses.

part3.q: What new technology excites you most right now?
part3.ref: Honestly, low-cost energy storage. Battery breakthroughs stretching electric buses further each year change air quality more than any trending app does. Also long-context AI assistants that remember your projects and deadlines — genuinely transformative for real work. Space launches thrill me, but boring infrastructure miracles like quiet motors and dead-cheap storage matter to people like us every single day.

part3.q: Do you think modern cities have become less friendly?
part3.ref: Superficially yes — everyone walks headphones-in and shares no eye contact. But look at weekend volunteer groups, community kitchens and neighbourhood rescue dogs. Friendliness in big cities moved from strangers in queues to chosen micro-communities. The friendship is there; the venue changed — from the market square to the group chat you chose on purpose.

part3.q: Do you believe celebrities have a responsibility to behave well?
part3.ref: Yes, simply because millions copy them. A singer who quits smoking publicly moves more behaviour than a hundred posters. But purity policing every influencer's private life is unfair and impossible. The reasonable line: public speech and profit-linked endorsements must carry honesty — no selling pills you wouldn't take, no campaigning on hollow values. Actions in public view, yes; sainthood, never.

part3.q: What role should grandparents play in raising children today?
part3.ref: Grandparents provide continuity — language, patience, unhurried meals, stories with no agenda. In many Chinese families they carry daily care while parents work long hours, which keeps costs survivable. The tension is between loving indulgence and modern discipline: grandparents soften rules at exactly the moment consistency matters most. Best: grandparents as warmth and memory, parents as boundary-setters, both at the table weekly.

part3.q: Is it true that people today are lonelier than before?
part3.ref: Surveys say yes — and so do my own eyes. Door delivery, single households, WFH and algorithmic feeds make 'social' life individualistic. But loneliness isn't cured by more people near you; it's cured by few real ones around you. Urban loneliness is worst among the young elderly and the over-connected. Designing weekly rituals with actual neighbours beats any chat-app membership.

part3.q: Do you think tipping culture will ever work in China?
part3.ref: Probably not — Chinese pricing culture bundles service into the listed price, and adding post-payment sums feels awkward here. Hong Kong and tourist districts run mixed models. Where quality differentiates, tips signal excellence without being mandatory. If Chinese consumers get transparent choice plus visibly better service for extra payment, fine; forced tipping screens at cafés will correctly annoy people like everyone.

part3.q: How important is punctuality in your society?
part3.ref: Extremely. In interviews, pitches and group projects, five minutes early is the baseline. But formality relaxes among friends — 8 pm dinner starts at 8:20 in many circles. The cost of lateness is trust erosion: colleagues quietly re-route around unreliable people regardless of talent. Being five minutes early solves 90 behaviour problems nobody else ever sees.

part3.q: Do you recycle at home, and why or why not?
part3.ref: Yes, mainly kitchen waste and paper. Our district fines non-compliance and the new bins are actually labelled with pictures now, so the learning curve is real. I don't always do it perfectly — festival packaging overwhelms everyone — but the habit now feels automatic, not virtuous. China recycled about 22 percent of municipal waste last year; it should be much higher by 2030.

part3.q: Should flights be taxed heavily to fight climate change?
part3.ref: A blanket flight tax punishes ordinary families, not the polluters. Smarter: frequent-flyer pricing where the first annual flights stay affordable, business class pays more, and short-haul routes under 800km face meaningful carbon levies. Also, taxing jet fuel, not tickets, targets actual emissions. Aviation decarbonisation needs money and fairness, not slogans.

part3.q: Will electric cars really solve city air pollution?
part3.ref: They solve tailpipe pollution, yes — my street feels measurably cleaner since half the courier bikes went electric. But total emissions depend on the grid mix: coal-heavy power just moves smoke to the upwind city. Real progress combines EVs, better buses, cycling lanes and shorter delivery chains. No single technology substitutes for urban design.

part3.q: Should companies be forced to reduce plastic packaging?
part3.ref: Yes, gradually and with teeth. Extended-producer-responsibility fees, banned microbeads, mandatory recycled content targets — these force redesign that one shopper's boycott never will. Companies respond fast when numbers bite. The current Chinese crackdown echoes the EU's 2021 single-use directive — same logic, good direction. Give industry five years, not ten, or we'll drown politely.

part3.q: What is the best way to encourage people to use public transport?
part3.ref: Make it faster, cheaper and kinder than the car, in that order. Dedicated bus lanes, metro expansion beyond tier-one cities, timetables that respect transfers, and stations with light, CCTV and clean toilets — these convert reluctant drivers more than posters ever will. Add congestion pricing on peak plates, and the math finally tips.

part3.q: Do you think fake news is a serious problem?
part3.ref: Yes, devastatingly. Health scares, election stories, disaster clips travel faster than corrections ever do. The damage lasts: vaccine hesitancy, financial panic, public distrust of legitimate journalism. Democracies now fund media-literacy curricula and verification hotlines — Sweden teaches schoolkids to fact-check TikTok. Technology will never fully solve it; citizen scepticism is the firewall.

part3.q: Should journalists have completely free speech, or limits?
part3.ref: Journalists deserve maximal speech protection plus maximal responsibility for accuracy. Libel law, source protection, right-to-reply — all fair. Publishing lies that endanger lives is not speech, it's sidearms. Independent press councils beat government censorship every time: they oversee conduct without owning the verdict. Free enough to challenge power, accountable enough to correct it.

part3.q: What role do influencers play in shaping public opinion?
part3.ref: Massive — often bigger than outlets for under-30s. A skincare influencer with 4 million followers moves product faster than any TV ad, and one malicious review can kill a brand in a day. Most influencers are educators without credentials or journalists without ethics training. Platforms should require disclosure, some literacy, and a verification track. Influence itself needs a licence plate.

part3.q: Is entertainment more important than education in the media today?
part3.ref: Yes, decisively. Entertainment feeds autoplay loops and ad revenue; education shows up when it entertains enough — think 200-episode documentaries or meme-based science accounts. The danger isn't that entertainment exists; it always did. It's that serious topics now have to disguise themselves as fun to be heard at all. Quality hides everywhere; make the boring thrilling and it wins.

part3.q: Should we trust what we read on social media less than traditional newspapers?
part3.ref: Absolutely, but with nuance. Quality newspapers maintain corrections, fact desks and named bylines — real accountability. Social media is a rumour engine unless the post is from a verified expert or primary source. The skill is triage: my rule is social media says 'what might be happening', newspaper says 'what did happen'. Treat feeds as hints, then verify with one good outlet.

part3.q: Do you think people today work longer hours than before?
part3.ref: Both true and hidden. Officially we work shorter weeks, but connectivity bleeds work into evenings — Slack pings at 10 pm, WeChat group demands on Sundays. Tech blurs every boundary until people feel always on. The rise of996 culture in China against a global push for four-day weeks tells you the fight is about attention, not just hours. True rest requires rules, not good intentions.

part3.q: Should everyone be forced to retire at a fixed age?
part3.ref: A rigid line ignores reality. Some 55-year-olds sprint while some 45-year-olds crawl; average health, role type and personal preference vary wildly. Flexible retirement with phased hours and strong pensions serves teams better. Mandatory age exits waste expertise and punish the healthy. Society needs gradual exits, not cliff edges — knowledge passed on through mentoring, not boxed away at midnight on a birthday.

part3.q: Is working from home good for employees or employers?
part3.ref: Both, when designed well: employees save commutes and deep focus; employers save space and widen talent pools internationally. The weakness is weak culture — new joiners miss the corridor osmosis learning from veterans. Hybrid models now win: two anchor days together, three remote for heads-down work. Trust-based home work beats surveillance-based home work every single time.

part3.q: Do you think salary or job satisfaction matters more when choosing work?
part3.ref: Salary buys stability; satisfaction buys years. Underpay skilled people and they leave by March; bored high earners burn out by year three. The smart default is competence plus meaning — you practise work you respect, for pay that respects you. Extremes both fail: starving for art demoralises; overpaid misery destroys health slowly. Compensation first for survival, satisfaction second for survival-of-the-soul.

part3.q: Should companies hire based on qualifications or practical experience?
part3.ref: Practical experience for 80 percent of roles. Degrees prove you can sit still and memorise; hands-on work proves you can ship. The exceptions are medicine and engineering, where foundations are non-negotiable. Modern hiring should weight portfolios, trials and referrals heavily — skills interviews over school prestige. Hire for evidence of behaviour, not paper promises of potential.

part3.q: How will offices change in the next decade?
part3.ref: Offices become clubs for collaboration, not warehouses for execution. Individual tasks move home permanently; the office sells whiteboards, workshops and unplanned serendipity. Floor plans shrink, booking systems rise, acoustic privacy becomes premium. The best offices will feel like creative hubs with coffee and silence zones — attendance by purpose, never by default.

part3.q: Is it important for young people to learn about their own culture?
part3.ref: Yes — cultural literacy is identity armour. Without knowing dumpling origins, dialect expressions and folk stories, young people drift into generic global consumers. Culture tells you who you are before you decide who to be. The trick is teaching it lively, not as test material: festivals as parties, dialects as comedy, history as mystery novels. Boring culture class creates resentment; living culture creates pride.

part3.q: How can governments protect traditional customs?
part3.ref: Fund living practice, not museums behind glass. Apprenticeships for craftspeople, festivals with real budgets, school visits with hands-on workshops, and tax relief for heritage businesses. UNESCO lists status helps visibility but money sustains survival. Protect customs by making them economically viable and emotionally fun — then young people choose them, not just preserve them out of guilt.

part3.q: Do you think modern lifestyles are destroying traditional culture?
part3.ref: Changing it, not destroying it. Global style dominates surfaces — coffee over tea in capsules, basketball over shuttlecock — but deep structure persists: Spring Festival travel, ancestral halls, zhong soup when sick. Cultures evolve or die; forced preservation produces theme parks. The question is not old versus new but meaningful versus disposable. Keep what teaches, adapt what feeds, drop what merely repeats.

part3.q: Should museums be free to enter?
part3.ref: Yes, like libraries — free entry is social infrastructure. Charges filter out exactly the curious poor who need them most. Funding can come from gift shops, memberships, tourist tickets and city budgets. The British Museum and Palace Museum prove accessibility works: attendance explodes when free, trust grows, education compounds. Pay the curators; waive the entrance gate.

part3.q: What is the value of art in everyday life?
part3.ref: Art trains the attention we waste on screens. A good poster makes you pause; a street violinist resets your commute; a subway mural teaches colour before language. Art democratises beauty — hospitals with paintings heal measurably faster. Everyone deserves culture without a ticket price. When cities invest in public art, they invest in citizens' mental health and civic pride simultaneously.

part3.q: Do you prefer spending money on experiences or possessions?
part3.ref: Experiences, decisively. Memories survive apartment moves and phone upgrades; objects depreciate and clutter. A weekend in Dali outlasts any jacket. That said, possessions like books, instruments and well-made tools earn their space by enabling more experiences. Spend on doing, not having — except the few things that upgrade every doing forever.

Today's lecture continues our series on consumer psychology, and the topic is festive consumption — what exactly happens to buying behaviour during December and the Lunar New Year season. Let me paint the overall picture first. Retail trade in December alone accounts for roughly 18 to 25 percent of annual turnover for many gift-and-food retailers, yet December is only about 8 percent of the calendar. Why is the gap so enormous?
The first mechanism is social signalling. Gifts are never just objects; they carry messages about relationship status, gratitude, and belonging. A 300-yuan gift to a colleague says 'we work well together'; an empty-handed visit to relatives implies indifference. Anthropologists call this the 'obligation to reciprocate' — once you receive, you must return something of comparable value, and the cycle compounds across the season.
The second mechanism is manufactured urgency. Shops run countdowns, limited editions and 'festival exclusives'. Neurologically, scarcity triggers loss aversion: the fear of missing out on something 'limited' peaks when time pressure is explicit — 48-hour offers, daily deal counts, stock counters. People buy not because they need the item, but because missing it feels like a loss.
Third: memory and identity. Festive consumption is ritual glue. The same sweets every year, the same empty candy tray refilled before guests arrive, the same box of longans from the same brand — these repetitions stabilise identity across generations. Children who watch their parents buy the same pineapple cake every New Year inherit not just a snack preference but a ritual map of 'what our family does'.
Now the numbers, briefly. In 2025, Chinese New Year spending during the golden week reached an estimated 1.2 trillion yuan, led by food, travel and digital red packets. Cross-border e-commerce saw a 30 percent spike in 'gift boxes' shipments. Research across cultures finds the same curve: festive peaks cluster around three categories — food and dinner parties, gifting, and experience purchases like cinema, travel and dining out.
So what are the practical consequences? For households: budget creep — people typically overspend by 15 to 30 percent during festive seasons versus ordinary months; set a written list before entering any supermarket. For young workers: financial stress peaks in January, so employers offering festive bonuses reduce anxiety more than equivalent salary in June. For retailers: the real competition starts in November, because habits are set early — early-bird buyers define the season's narrative.
Finally, a reflective note. Not all of this is pathology. Festive spending supports millions of livelihoods — artisans, shopkeepers, delivery drivers, caterers. The healthy stance is conscious participation: celebrate, but with a deliberate list, a real budget, and one moment of asking 'is this gift for them, or for how I want to look?' That single question cuts unnecessary spending by roughly a fifth in our survey data. Next lecture: the psychology of hospitality — why 'the more you host, the more you show'.

questions.explain: 原文：'is this gift for them, or for how I want to look?' ... cuts unnecessary spending by roughly a fifth。

part1.q: Do you have any special holidays coming up soon?
part1.ref: Yes, Spring Festival is coming up in February. My company gives us seven days off this year, so my plan is to go back to my grandparents' village for the first few days and simply rest, eat well and see relatives I haven't met since last year.

part1.q: How do you usually spend your holidays?
part1.ref: Mostly around family. We have a big dinner on New Year's Eve, sleep in until noon for a couple of days, and then take one short trip somewhere — last year we went to Hangzhou for the lantern festival by West Lake.

part1.q: Which is your favourite holiday of the year?
part1.ref: Without question, Spring Festival. The whole city slows down, every restaurant serves family reunion banquets, and you get this rare feeling that everyone is home at the same time — it feels like the one week when the country actually rests.

part1.q: Do you prefer holidays at home or travelling?
part1.ref: It depends on the length. For three or four days, travelling is tempting, but Spring Festival crowds make trains exhausting, so I usually just stay home for the peak days and save travelling for the quiet weeks afterwards.

part1.q: Do you think people nowadays take enough holidays?
part1.ref: Legally, yes, but in practice many people don't use their full allowance. Some feel guilty taking time off, and others simply cannot escape work messages. Resting properly should be a skill we teach, not a luxury people apologise for.

part1.q: Do you enjoy giving gifts to your friends?
part1.ref: I really do. Choosing a gift forces you to pay attention — you remember what someone mentioned weeks ago. Last autumn I noticed a colleague kept admiring a certain teapot, so I found the exact one for her birthday.

part1.q: What is the most memorable gift you have ever received?
part1.ref: A fountain pen from my grandfather when I finished university. It wasn't expensive, but he'd repaired cars for forty years and this was the pen he'd used to sign every contract. It means more to me than anything money could buy.

part1.q: Do you prefer giving gifts or receiving them?
part1.ref: Giving, honestly. Receiving is pleasant, but the real joy is watching someone's face when they realise the gift truly shows you know them — that gap between 'they got me something' and 'they really get me' is everything.

part1.q: How do you usually choose a gift for someone?
part1.ref: I start with their habits, not their wish list. I ask myself: what do they complain about, what do they light up over, what did they almost buy? A good gift answers one of those three questions better than they could themselves.

part1.q: Is gift-giving important in your culture?
part1.ref: Extremely. During Spring Festival we exchange red envelopes, gift boxes of tea, fruit or nuts, and nobody shows up empty-handed to a relative's home. Gifts there are not really about objects — they're a way of saying 'I value this relationship enough to think about you'.

part1.q: What do you usually eat for breakfast?
part1.ref: Something simple — soy milk and a couple of eggs, or congee from the breakfast shop downstairs when I'm running late. I used to skip breakfast entirely, but I get headaches by 11 am now if I do.

part1.q: Do you prefer eating at home or eating in restaurants?
part1.ref: Mostly home. Cooking for myself is cheaper and I control the salt and oil, which I care about. Restaurants are for occasions — birthdays, reunions — when the cooking itself is part of the celebration rather than just feeding people.

part1.q: What was your favourite meal when you were a child?
part1.ref: My mother's soup dumplings on Sunday mornings — little pork parcels you had to eat with the skin in one bite, burning your tongue every single time. I still think about that texture when food gets stressful at work.

part1.q: Do you think people eat too much fast food these days?
part1.ref: Absolutely, and mostly for time reasons rather than taste. When you're ordering at 9 pm after a double shift, a burger beats chopping vegetables every time. The problem is when it becomes every meal, because then sodium and fried oil compound quietly for years.

part1.q: What would your ideal dinner be?
part1.ref: Hotpot, without question — a pot of bubbling broth in the middle, everyone reaching for a dipping bowl, arguing over which meat went in too soon. It's chaotic, loud and social, which is exactly what eating should be more often than it is.

part1.q: How do you usually spend your weekends?
part1.ref: Slow mornings for sure — I never set an alarm on Saturdays. Then gym or a long walk, one proper meal cooked at home, and either a film or meeting friends in the evening. Sundays are for laundry, tidying and preparing the week so Monday doesn't bite.

part1.q: Do you have the same routine every weekend?
part1.ref: Roughly. The skeleton stays the same — sleep in, one outing, one good meal — but the middle is flexible. Some weekends I hike with friends, others I just plant myself on the sofa with a book and call it self-care.

part1.q: What did you do last weekend?
part1.ref: We drove to a suburban IKEA in the morning — yes, it's basically a sport at this point — then had hotpot for lunch. In the afternoon I repotted two dying houseplants and somehow resurrected one of them. Small victory.

part1.q: Would you like to have more free time on weekends?
part1.ref: Everyone would, but I'd probably fill it badly. Two days off sounds ideal until you remember half of it evaporates into errands. Maybe I'd rather have one proper four-day break per season than endless flat weekends that blur into laundry.

part1.q: Do you think weekends are important?
part1.ref: Completely. They're where your nervous system resets. Without weekends, the week becomes one long Tuesday, and you start making strange decisions like buying espresso machines you'll never use. Rest is not the reward for work; it's the fuel for it.

part1.q: Do you live with your family?
part1.ref: I live with my parents and my grandmother in the same apartment block — different units, which keeps everyone sane. In a way it's the classic Chinese three-generation setup, just with more delivery food and video calls than the old days.

part1.q: Who in your family do you spend the most time with?
part1.ref: My mother, overwhelmingly. She cooks when she visits, reorganises my bookshelf without asking, and somehow knows when I'm stressed before I do. She denies it is hovering; I call it loving surveillance.

part1.q: Did your family eat dinner together when you were young?
part1.ref: Almost every night. My father would wait until seven, then make us put our phones in a drawer — which felt oppressive at fourteen and feels heroic at twenty-eight. Those dinners were where I learned half of what I know about storytelling.

part1.q: Are you similar to or different from the other members of your family?
part1.ref: I'm the quiet one — my brother talks for a living, my mother narrates everything, and my father operates in meaningful silence. I inherited the silence but not the patience for long monologues, so I usually retreat into books.

part1.q: Have your family habits changed over the years?
part1.ref: Noticeably. Ten years ago we'd sit at the same table arguing about the news; now the news competes with two TikTok feeds and a WeChat sports group. We eat together, yes — but silence has a different flavour when everyone is scrolling.

part1.q: Do you like watching films?
part1.ref: Hugely. Cinema is my monthly ritual — I don't even check the reviews anymore, I just trust the opening weekend vibe. The big-screen experience does something a laptop can never replicate for fight scenes and soundtracks.

part1.q: What kinds of films do you enjoy most?
part1.ref: Light comedies and character-driven dramas. I tried hard-core arthouse once and lasted forty minutes before checking into a thriller I actually enjoyed. Life is already complicated enough; my popcorn budget deserves a happy ending occasionally.

part1.q: When was the last time you went to the cinema?
part1.ref: Last month — we saw a sci-fi epic that was mostly visual spectacle, which is exactly what cinema should be. Tickets plus popcorn plus parking came to over 150 yuan, and I regretted none of it.

part1.q: Do you prefer watching films at home or at the cinema?
part1.ref: Home wins for comfort — pause anytime, no noisy strangers, whatever snack I want — but cinema wins for spectacle. So my rule is simple: if it's a visual feast, big screen; if it's dialogue-heavy, sofa and a cup of tea.

part1.q: Have your tastes in films changed over time?
part1.ref: Completely. Teenage me wanted explosions every ten minutes; adult me cries at reunion scenes in quiet family dramas and tolerates action only when the choreography is genuinely clever. Growing up apparently recalibrates your dopamine.

part1.q: Do you like chocolate?
part1.ref: Very much, but I've graduated from milk chocolate to dark chocolate over the years. Now I treat chocolate like coffee — a small square after dinner, not a bar in front of the TV at midnight.

part1.q: How often do you eat chocolate?
part1.ref: Realistically two or three times a week. Weekends are the danger zone — a film night with a proper bar is my one indulgence. Weekdays I'm better behaved, mostly due to the 70-percent rule I pretend to follow.

part1.q: What kind of chocolate do you prefer?
part1.ref: Dark, 70 percent or above, preferably with sea salt or orange peel. Milk chocolate tastes like dessert; dark chocolate tastes like an opinion. Nuts are acceptable; nougat and caramel are traps I walk into knowingly.

part1.q: Was chocolate popular when you were a child?
part1.ref: Enormously — it was the currency of good behaviour. Every Spring Festival, the table would fill up with boxes of chocolates and fruit, and we kids treated the chocolate box as a competitive sport. Now those gift boxes are pricier than ever.

part1.q: Do you think chocolate is healthy?
part1.ref: Dark chocolate in small amounts, honestly, yes — the flavanol headlines are partly true. But the moment it becomes three bars a week it's dessert with a marketing department. Everything about food is dose and context, as my nutritionist keeps reminding me.

part1.q: Do you like travelling?
part1.ref: Very much. Technically, two weeks of holidays a year is all I get, so I've learned to do intense short trips — three days somewhere with one good meal, one good walk and one strange museum beats a two-week blur every time.

part1.q: Where did you travel most recently?
part1.ref: Xitang, the water town near Shanghai, this autumn. We rented a little guesthouse by the canal, ate zongzi for breakfast, took the boat ride at dusk, and got caught in sudden rain — which honestly made it better.

part1.q: Do you prefer travelling alone or with other people?
part1.ref: With others, because shared anticipation is half the fun — splitting the map, arguing about dinner, sending each other photos. Alone travelling sounds romantic until you're eating noodles by yourself and checking the same fork menu for the tenth time.

part1.q: What kind of places do you most enjoy visiting?
part1.ref: Old towns and mountains. Old towns give me layered history frozen into streets — a bit of Ming architecture, a bit of Qing signage — and mountains give me silence and altitude, which is the closest my city life ever gets to meditation.

part1.q: Would you like to travel abroad in the future?
part1.ref: Yes, very much — Japan first, then maybe Italy for the architecture and the food. I've been saving points and pretending it's 'for emergencies' while quietly researching ryokans instead. Next year, realistically, if the budget cooperates.

part2.card: Describe a gift you gave to someone.
points: When and why you gave it
part2.ref: Last New Year I gave my mother a fountain pen — actually, not just any pen, but the same model of pen my grandfather used to sign his first shop contract. She has run the family eatery for fifteen years, and every New Year she writes the year's first menu by hand in ink. When I handed it to her on Chinese New Year's Eve, she went quiet, then laughed and said 'this one actually lasts'. She still opens it only for that first menu of each year, which makes it worth every minute I spent hunting down an original.

part2.card: Describe a member of your family you get on very well with.
points: And explain why you get on so well
part2.ref: This is my grandmother, Nai, who will be eighty-two this spring. We do almost everything together — she reads the evening paper aloud, correcting her own reading; we shell peanuts while the Spring Festival gala plays; she teaches me card games from the old countryside. She is sharp, stubborn in the best way, and completely without embarrassment. We get on because she treats me as a colleague in life rather than a child to manage. I can tell her anything, and she has never once told my mother.

part2.card: Describe a happy event you remember from your childhood.
points: And explain why it was so happy
part2.ref: The happiest day of my childhood was the afternoon our family moved from a two-room walk-up into our own apartment — new keys, new elevator, and a balcony. I was nine. My father celebrated with a tray of strawberries, which were absurdly expensive that year, and we ate them sitting on the empty floor. What made it unforgettable wasn't the apartment itself; it was watching my parents exhale for the first time I had ever seen. I still remember the hum of the empty fridge and strawberry-stained hands.

part2.card: Describe a memorable shopping experience you had.
points: What you bought or shopped for
And explain what made it memorable
part2.ref: I'll never forget hunting for a Spring Festival coat with my mother at a small market in Chengdu last January. It was chaos — steam from spicy-hotpot stalls, bargaining over wool blends, a vendor playing erhu over the loudspeaker. After two hours I found a deep green wool coat, half the asking price, and the vendor finally smiled and said 'you have an eye — take it'. Wearing it home on the metro felt like I'd won a treasure rather than bought a jacket.

part2.card: Describe a weekend you really enjoyed.
points: Where you went or what you did
And explain why it was enjoyable
part2.ref: This was the winter weekend in December 2023 when the whole family drove to the reservoir for a 'fake fishing' day — actually barbecuing, playing mahjong in the car, and watching black kites circling over the far shore. My aunt brought some homemade dumplings, my cousin taught my grandmother to use a tablet, and nobody looked at a work message for two entire days. It was enjoyable because it was ordinary abundance — no agenda, no itinerary, just shared morning light and too much food.

part3.q: Should schools have longer holidays?
part3.ref: Longer holidays would give children breathing room, but the real question is what they do with the time. Unstructured weeks can widen gaps between privileged and poor students — the former travel, the latter drift. Longer holidays work best paired with structured camps, reading programmes and proper rest culture at home.

part3.q: Do you think homework should be banned during holidays?
part3.ref: Banned entirely is too blunt, but reduced drastically, yes. Holiday homework that replaces rest with more worksheets teaches resentment, not learning. Better: one open-ended project you choose yourself — a family interview, a photo essay, cooking one new dish — because autonomy beats obligation for retaining anything meaningful.

part3.q: Is it important for children to learn about festivals from other cultures?
part3.ref: Deeply. Festivals compress a culture's values into one edible, shareable day — learning Thanksgiving, Diwali or Eid teaches food ethics, gratitude and solidarity better than any textbook. It also vaccinates against casual prejudice; knowing why someone fasts changes how you sit next to them at lunch.

part3.q: Do exams really show what a student can do?
part3.ref: Only a slice of it. Exams are excellent at measuring preparation under pressure, but they miss collaboration, creativity, persistence and practical judgment. The fix isn't abandoning exams — it's balancing them with projects, orals and portfolios so a quiet builder doesn't lose to a loud test-taker.

part3.q: Should universities help students find jobs after graduation?
part3.ref: Yes — a degree should be a launchpad, not just a certificate. Career coaching, CV workshops, alumni networks and mock interviews convert academic knowledge into employability. When universities treat careers as someone else's job, students graduate with skills and no map. Employability support is part of the product now.

part3.q: What can adults learn that children cannot?
part3.ref: Adults learn with context. A child memorises vocabulary; an adult connects it to a negotiation, a lease or a lover's apology — that stakes-driven learning sticks harder. Adults also tolerate ambiguity better, ask sharper questions and accept feedback without collapsing. Motivation matures along with the corpus of scars.

part3.q: Should there be limits on children's screen time during holidays?
part3.ref: Reasonable limits, not bans. Holidays are about rest, and screens genuinely rest tired brains — but three hours of short video is sedation, not rest. My household rule: mornings are physical, afternoons are free, evenings are co-screened film nights. Quality and context outrank raw timer counts.

part3.q: Will delivery apps make festive cooking obsolete?
part3.ref: For everyday meals maybe, but festivals survive on slowness. The point of making dumplings for Spring Festival dinner is the hours together around the table — no courier can deliver that feeling. Apps will compress weekday cooking, but ritual cooking during holidays will persist precisely because it is inefficient and human.

part3.q: Is online shopping good or bad for local businesses during holidays?
part3.ref: Both at once. Online shopping gives micro-vendors national reach for festive gifts, but it bulldozes the family-run shop on the corner that survives on seasonal traffic. The healthy model is omnichannel — local shops using WeChat stores and delivery, plus physical experience during festive peaks.

part3.q: Do smart homes actually make life easier?
part3.ref: For daily chores, yes — lights, locks and robot vacuums genuinely compress effort. But every smart device is also a small subscription to someone else's server: accounts expire, apps vanish, privacy quietly evaporates. Use smart tech for chores you hate, keep manual backups for the things you love — including the kettle.

part3.q: Should AI be allowed to write greeting cards and wishes?
part3.ref: It can draft, but humans must sign. A wish matters because someone paused to think about you — if AI writes it, the gift arrives without the sender ever having been present in the message. The lovely use of AI is brainstorming lines for the shy, not replacing the feeling itself.

part3.q: How will robots change hospitality in the future?
part3.ref: Robots will absorb the repetitive backbone — towel delivery, table clearing, check-in at 3 am — and free humans for the moments that actually matter: calming a crying child, remembering a returning guest's tea. Hospitality will split into invisible automation and high-touch warmth; the middle ground will disappear entirely.

part3.q: Does modern life leave enough space for family time?
part3.ref: Technically yes, culturally no. We have more time than our grandparents did, yet family time gets fragmented into notification slices. The bottleneck isn't hours, it's attention. Households that succeed treat dinner as a device-free zone — twenty minutes of full presence beats three distracted hours every time.

part3.q: Should governments mandate paid public holidays?
part3.ref: Paid holidays are already mandated almost everywhere — the question is enforcement and fairness across gig work. Delivery riders and factory shift workers often can't stop, even when the law says they can. A public holiday you cannot take is decoration, not policy. Extend coverage to contract and gig workers first.

part3.q: Is traditional community spirit disappearing in big cities?
part3.ref: It mutated rather than vanished. The old courtyard gossip moved to WeChat groups of neighbours sharing matcha reviews and lost-cat alerts. What's missing is accidental encounter — corridor hellos, shared queues, borrowed ladders. Design must now engineer serendipity: shared tables, open kitchens, co-working lobbies, festivals in the square.

part3.q: Do older people get the respect they deserve in China today?
part3.ref: Formally yes — filial duty is still preached — but structurally it's eroding. Nuclear families, migration to tier-one cities and youthful consumer culture leave many elderly invisible in daily life. Respect needs practice, not posters: shared meals, real conversations, elders teaching craft and stories, not just being 'cared for'.

part3.q: Should festivals be public holidays for everyone or regional only?
part3.ref: Regional festivals are precious precisely because they're not national — dragon boat races in the south, lantern fairs in the west. Making everything a national holiday flattens local culture into a single televised script. Better: national core holidays plus regional floating rest days that let local identity breathe.

part3.q: Is it true that people are more stressed during holiday seasons?
part3.ref: For many, yes — travel chaos, family friction, gift budgets, forced fun. Festive pressure is a documented cortisol bump. The antidote is expectation management: fewer dinners, honest conversations, pre-agreed budgets, and the radical act of doing nothing on purpose with people you like.

part3.q: Do festive celebrations create too much waste?
part3.ref: Yes, dramatically — wrapping paper, fruit baskets with non-recyclable foam, disposable tableware for reunion dinners. The fix isn't cancelling joy; it's swapping materials. Beeswax wraps, steel lanterns, reusable plates, shared platters — every festive choice can whisper 'celebrate, but gently' instead of shouting 'landfill'.

part3.q: Should fireworks be banned completely?
part3.ref: Partial bans work; total bans breed black markets and resentment. The honest approach: restrict in dense cities, subsidise eco-friendly drones or light shows, and let rural towns keep tradition with moderation. Smoke over Beijing is bad air; light over a village square is culture. Regulate the dose, not the desire.

part3.q: Is holiday travel compatible with carbon budgets?
part3.ref: Only if travel patterns shift, not disappear. One long-haul trip a year plus regional rail holidays is reasonable for most people. Flying short-haul when high-speed rail exists is hard to justify on any honest carbon ledger. Choose slower journeys — the extra six hours on a train is the price of a quieter conscience.

part3.q: Should gift culture move toward experiences instead of objects?
part3.ref: Mostly yes — a museum membership or a cooking class outlives any box of trinkets, and it keeps money circulating in local culture. But objects have their place: a handmade scarf is still love in fabric form. The healthy mix is experiences first, meaningful objects second, plastic novelties never.

part3.q: How can cities become greener during festive seasons?
part3.ref: LED installations instead of incandescent bulbs, real potted trees instead of plastic forests, pedestrian-only promenades, shared e-bike fleets for the last mile. Cities already compete on their festive light shows — let the competition be about kilowatt-hours saved rather than watts dazzled.

part3.q: Does festive advertising manipulate consumers unfairly?
part3.ref: Absolutely — it sells obligation wrapped as love. The message is always: 'you don't really care unless you buy this'. Awareness is the defence; when you see an ad and feel vague guilt, that is the emotion being engineered, not affection. Buy for people, not for ads.

part3.q: Is the Spring Festival Gala still relevant to young people?
part3.ref: Partly. It's ritual background music for the reunion dinner — less watched for content, more for the shared clock. Young audiences prefer highlight clips on Douyin, yet the live viewership still spikes at midnight. Its role shifted from 'must-watch programme' to 'national gathering signal' — different, but alive.

part3.q: Should news channels avoid broadcasting during major holidays?
part3.ref: No — holidays are exactly when major events happen: weather crises, travel disasters, accidents. What should change is tone: fewer panels of pundits, more service journalism — road closures, weather alerts, hospital schedules. News during festivals should be a lighthouse, not a shouting match.

part3.q: Do holiday movies make us feel better?
part3.ref: For most people, genuinely yes. Comfort rewatching — the same Home Alone, the same sentimental reunion dramas — regulates mood the way a warm blanket does. The danger is only when comfort becomes avoidance; a film a night is self-care, five films a day is hiding from your family with a remote.

part3.q: How honest is influencer content about holiday lifestyle?
part3.ref: Mostly curated theatre. The 'perfect family reunion dinner' on Douyin is twelve takes, rented dishes and ring-light negotiation. Some influencers now do behind-the-scenes honesty about this, and those videos build real trust. Enjoy the fantasy, but calibrate expectations — your real aunt will never pose like that.

part3.q: Should companies be forced to give staff bonuses before Spring Festival?
part3.ref: Mandating bonuses would help cash-poor employees in a culture where the holiday is expensive — but one-size bonuses punish good companies and subsidise bad ones. Better: tax incentives for festive bonuses, transparency requirements, and strong enforcement of existing bonus promises in contracts.

part3.q: Is the nine-nine-six work culture still tolerable today?
part3.ref: Tolerated by many, embraced by fewer every year. 996 trades health and family for equity and speed — a bad deal for most roles outside early-stage startups. The backlash is real: regulators, courts and talent are all pushing back. Sustainable pace wins in the long run; burnout is not a moat.

part3.q: Do people really rest during holidays if they work from home?
part3.ref: Rarely fully. Remote work means the laptop is always within reach, and 'checking in' for five minutes becomes two hours of emails. True rest needs boundaries: out-of-office replies, silenced groups, and a household agreement that holiday hours belong to the people in the room.

part3.q: Should interns and part-timers get paid holidays too?
part3.ref: Yes — proportional leave is basic fairness. If a student works three months before Spring Festival, they've earned some release time. Hospitality, retail and delivery rely on these workers exactly at the festive peak. Paying only 'full staff' treats half the workforce as disposable; proportional rights fix most of that gap.

part3.q: Will the gig economy change how holidays feel in China?
part3.ref: It's changing them already — riders, drivers and couriers work through every festival while office towers empty. Festive convenience is built on invisible labour. Society should either guarantee festive pay multipliers and rest for gig workers, or stop pretending holidays are restful for everyone equally.

part3.q: Is career success defined by money or meaning by 2026?
part3.ref: For young Chinese professionals the honest answer is both, in tension — money buys security, meaning buys sleep. The post-2020 generation increasingly optimises for 'enough money plus work that doesn't hollow me out'. Hustle culture lost some shine; sustainable ambition is the new status signal.

part3.q: Are traditional festivals becoming too commercial?
part3.ref: Commercialisation amplifies festivals without fully replacing them. The shopping pressure is real, yet the core rituals — ancestor visits, reunion dinners, red envelopes — persist precisely because they're emotional infrastructure, not products. The test for each festival is simple: would this still happen if nobody made money from it? Spring Festival passes.

part3.q: Should young people learn festive rituals if they feel meaningless?
part3.ref: Yes — but as lived experience, not lecture. Rituals only feel hollow when learned as obligations; they bloom when children cook, paste couplets and light lamps alongside elders. Meaning is negotiated in the doing. Teach the motion and the reasons will follow.

part3.q: Is Lunar New Year more important than Christmas in China today?
part3.ref: Culturally yes, commercially close. Lunar New Year is the national heartbeat — family, food, homecoming — while Christmas has become a lifestyle festival of lights and shopping without religious weight. Both coexist easily: December for aesthetics and dates, February for the soul of the country.

part3.q: How should museums make festivals relevant for schools?
part3.ref: By making festivals hands-on: dumpling workshops, lantern-making labs, story corners where elders speak. Museums should be loud during festival weeks, not silent — food smells, soundscapes, costume try-ons. A museum a child remembers beats a worksheet about heritage every single time.

part3.q: Will global culture erase local festivals eventually?
part3.ref: No — local festivals are stubborn precisely because they're embodied: the foods, the firecrackers, the dialects. Globalisation adds layers, it doesn't bleach them. The real risk is insider apathy: young people who can't be bothered. Keep festivals edible, participatory and slightly chaotic, and they will outlive every trend.

part3.q: What do festivals teach children that schools cannot?
part3.ref: Festivals teach belonging. No syllabus delivers the feeling of thirty relatives arguing happily over mahjong in one room and a pot too big to lift alone. They transmit values non-verbally — generosity, endurance, patience, memory — through repetition of shared action. Schools inform; festivals initiate.
